## Expectations for submitted work

- Homeworks are assessed for **completion** and **effort**.
   - Address all parts of questions completely whenever you can. If you have a partial solution, say so, explain what you've tried.
   - Respond in [full sentences]{.underline} for written answers, and explain your reasoning.
   - Show your work, not just your final answer/value.
   - Code in submitted assignments should run (not be commented out whenever possible) and include a clear attempt to address the question.

<br>

- Quizzes are assessed for **accuracy**.
   - Similar expectations apply: respond in full sentences that address all parts of problems, explain your reasoning, show your work. 
    
------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Expectations for submitted work
   
- **Collaboration**:
    - An excellent way to deepen your understanding and enjoy the learning experience
    - You should try all problems on your own first
    - Can involve comparison of reasoning and solutions when each student has attempted a problem
    - Should **never** involve direct sharing or copying of solutions
    - Should be guided by the honor principle

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Engagement

#### Technology policy

<br>

::: blockquote

In STAT 141, we value a focused, distraction-free environment. Personal devices (including phones and headphones) and computers are generally not allowed in **lecture** to minimize digital distractions. However, technology is welcome for students who require digital tools for accessibility. We ask that these students limit their device use to essential in-class activities, such as note-taking or viewing digital readings. Non-academic use—including social media, messaging, and general web browsing—is not allowed, to ensure we remain fully engaged with the course material. Note that all lecture slides will be made available ahead of lecture on the course website.

:::

## Engagement

  
-   I have high expectations but know that all of you (regardless of your stats, math, or computing background) have the ability to meet them.

-   We are all going to make mistakes, we will learn more because of them.

-   Resilience is one of the most valuable **skills** in learning.

------------------------------------------------------------------------


## Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy


::: blockquote

Artificial intelligence (AI) tools, such as ChatGPT, Claude, Co-Pilot, Gemini, and others are being used to generate code, analyze data, and much more. However, learning to think critically about a problem at hand, building resilience in moments of struggle and confusion, and engaging with your peers, tutors, and instructors when not understanding a concept or question are integral components of a liberal arts education. Further, a key goal of this course is for you to learn how to thoughtfully, ethically, and **independently** extract knowledge from data and engage in statistical reasoning. Therefore, the use of generative AI tools, such as ChatGPT and others, are strictly prohibited in any stage of the work process for this course. The [Honor Principle](https://www.reed.edu/honor_principle/) must guide your conduct in following this policy. If you have questions about whether a tool is allowed for this course, ask before using it.

If you are unsure of how to approach a particular exercise on an assignment, or are stuck on a concept from lecture, help is available to you! Please visit office hours, collaborate with your peers, or post in the Slack channel.

:::

## Statistical Thinking

-   About developing **reasoning** (not just learning definitions and formulae).

-   Statistical thinking requires **judgment** that takes time to develop.
    -   Will see **examples** and **practice** applying statistical thinking throughout the course.
    - Numeric calculations only get us so far: it is critical to understand the **underlying data** and **assumptions**

-   Developing our statistical thinking skills will allow us to soundly **extract knowledge from data**!

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## [What are/is Data?]{.center}

<br>

<br>

::: blockquote
[*"'Raw data' is an oxymoron."* -- Lisa Gitelman](https://catalog.library.reed.edu/permalink/01ALLIANCE_REED/ivkaaq/alma99900791224501841)
:::

<br>

::: blockquote
[*"Data ... is information made tractable."* -- Catherine D'Ignazio and Lauren Klein](https://catalog.library.reed.edu/permalink/01ALLIANCE_REED/ivkaaq/alma99900435411901841)
:::

## Data Frames

Data in **spreadsheet**-like format where:

-   Rows = Observations/cases

-   Columns = Variables

```{r}
#| echo: false
# pak::pak("simonpcouch/detectors")
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(detectors)

detectors %>%
  mutate(ID = row_number()) %>%
  relocate(ID) %>%
  select(-document_id, -prompt) %>%
  head() %>%

  kable() %>%   
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("responsive", "bordered", "striped", "compact"),
                font_size = 32)

```

-   Data from **GPT Detectors Are Biased Against Non-Native English Writers.** *Weixin Liang*, *Mert Yuksekgonul*, *Yining Mao*, *Eric Wu*, *James Zou.* [CellPress Patterns](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patter.2023.100779) and available in the `R` package `detectors`.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Rows = Observations/cases

**What are the cases? What does each row represent?**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Data Frames

```{r}
#| echo: false

detectors %>%
  mutate(ID = row_number()) %>%
  relocate(ID) %>%
  select(-document_id, -prompt) %>%
  head() %>%

  kable() %>%   
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("responsive", "bordered", "striped", "compact"),
                font_size = 32)

```

Columns = Variables

**Variables**: Describe characteristics of the observations

-   **Quantitative**: Numerical in nature

-   **Categorical**: Values are categories

-   **Identification**: Uniquely identify each case

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Data Frames

```{r}
#| echo: false

detectors %>%
  mutate(ID = row_number()) %>%
  relocate(ID) %>%
  select(-document_id, -prompt) %>%
  head() %>%

  kable() %>%   
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("responsive", "bordered", "striped", "compact"),
                font_size = 32)

```

Every time you get a new dataset, spend time exploring the variables.

::: {.fragment style="font-size: 0.9em;"}

**Example questions**:

-   Is each variable capturing the desired information?

-   For categorical variables, what are the categories? Do those categories adequately represent that variable?

-   For quantitative variables, what values are possible? Were the data rounded or binned? Are those values actually encoding categories? What are the units of measurement?

:::
